questions.question: A triangle has three angles. Two of the angles measure 60° and 70°. Remember that the three angles inside any triangle add up to 180° in total. What is the measure of the third angle?
questions.explain: Add the two known angles (60° + 70° = 130°), then subtract from the 180° total: 180° − 130° = 50°. A common trap is stopping at 130°, which is just the sum of the two angles you were given, not the missing one.

questions.question: A triangle has one right angle that measures 90°. A second angle in the same triangle measures 35°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. What is the measure of the third angle?
questions.explain: Add the two known angles (90° + 35° = 125°) and subtract from 180°, giving 180° − 125° = 55°. Watch out for subtracting only one angle: 180° − 35° = 145° forgets that the right angle also uses up part of the 180°.

questions.question: A triangle has two angles that each measure 45°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180° in total. What is the measure of the third angle, and what kind of angle is it?
questions.explain: 45° + 45° = 90°, and 180° − 90° = 90°, which is exactly a right angle. Using 360° instead of 180° gives 270° — that whole-turn total belongs to quadrilaterals, not triangles.

questions.question: A triangle has one angle that measures 100° and another that measures 32°. All three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. What is the measure of the missing angle?
questions.explain: Add the known angles first (100° + 32° = 132°), then do 180° − 132° = 48°. Subtracting just one angle, like 180° − 100° = 80°, leaves the 32° angle out of the calculation.

questions.question: Nika builds a four-sided kite for the beach at Spanish Banks. Three of its angles measure 95°, 80° and 110°. What is the measure of the fourth angle of her kite?
questions.explain: A quadrilateral has four angles that add to 360°, so add the three known angles (95° + 80° + 110° = 285°) and subtract: 360° − 285° = 75°. The trap is using 180°, the triangle total, or forgetting to subtract all three angles.

questions.question: The triangular sail on a boat in Deep Cove has one angle of 38° at the bottom and another of 27° at the top. What is the measure of the sail's third angle?
questions.explain: The angles of a triangle total 180°: 38° + 27° = 65°, and 180° − 65° = 115°. Choosing 65° means you only found the sum of the two given angles and stopped before subtracting.

questions.question: Jaya is making a triangular banner for her class. Two of its angles measure 55° and 65°, so she writes the equation x + 55 + 65 = 180 to find the missing angle x. What is the value of x?
questions.explain: Combine the numbers first: x + 120 = 180, so x = 180 − 120 = 60°. A common slip is answering 120°, which is only the part of the 180° already used up by the two known angles.

questions.question: A tabletop at a Surrey library is shaped like a quadrilateral. Two of its corners are square corners measuring 90° each, and a third corner measures 65°. What is the measure of the fourth corner?
questions.explain: The four angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, so 90° + 90° + 65° = 245° and 360° − 245° = 115°. Using the triangle total of 180° here is the usual mistake — four-sided shapes need 360°.

questions.question: Ravi cuts a triangular piece of cedar shingle. The angle at the top of the piece measures 40°, and the other two angles are equal to each other. What is the measure of each of those two equal angles?
questions.explain: First find what is left of the 180°: 180° − 40° = 140°. Because the two remaining angles are equal, split that leftover in half: 140° ÷ 2 = 70°. Answering 140° is the most common error — that is the two angles together, not each one.

questions.question: A window frame at a Kelowna school is shaped like a quadrilateral. Three of its angles measure 90°, 90° and 130°. What is the fourth angle, and how would you classify it?
questions.explain: Add the known angles (90° + 90° + 130° = 310°) and subtract from 360° to get 50°, which is less than 90° and therefore acute. An angle only counts as obtuse when it is between 90° and 180°, and as reflex when it is more than 180°.
